# Appendix: Running the local model from the USB key

A USB key distributed in session carries a portable install of
[llama.cpp](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp) with the **Ling-3.0-tiny**
model, ready to serve an OpenAI-compatible API on your machine. This appendix
gives the exact launch commands for Windows and macOS, explains how to tune the
server when a machine is low on VRAM, and shows how to connect the server to
Zed.

The model card is <https://huggingface.co/inclusionAI/Ling-3.0-tiny>. The GGUF
files are published at <https://huggingface.co/bloomer010/Ling-3.0-tiny-GGUF>.

## What the key contains

```text
usb-llama/
├── model/
│   └── Ling-3.0-tiny-Q4_K_M.gguf   # the model, ~4.5 GB
├── mac-arm64/                      # macOS Apple Silicon (Metal GPU)
├── mac-x64/                        # macOS Intel (CPU)
├── win-vulkan/                     # Windows, Vulkan GPU
├── win-cpu/                        # Windows, CPU
├── run-mac.command                 # macOS: double-click
├── run-mac.sh                      # macOS: launch from a terminal
├── run-windows.bat                 # Windows: double-click
└── README.md                       # quick guide (in French)
```

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Model | Ling-3.0-tiny |
| Architecture | Sparse mixture-of-experts (bailingmoe3) |
| Parameters | 7.9B total, 1.3B active per token |
| Context window | 256K native (262,144 tokens), output up to 32,768 tokens |
| Quantization | Q4_K_M (~4.5 GB file) |
| Languages | English, Chinese |
| llama.cpp build | b10639 (includes bailingmoe3 support) |

Hardware expectations match [Option 3](prerequisites.qmd) of the prerequisites:
about 16 GB of RAM, or a GPU with ~6 GB of VRAM for the offload settings below.
At Q4_K_M the whole model fits in memory; the server also reserves memory for the
conversation context, which grows with the `-c` value.

## Copy the folder first

The USB key transports the folder; do not run anything from it. Copy the whole
folder to your disk (Desktop, Documents, …) and launch the server from that local
copy. The key is formatted exFAT, which both Windows and macOS read; the folder
works identically once copied.

## Starting the server

### macOS

Double-click `run-mac.command`. If macOS blocks the double-click, open a
Terminal in the folder and run `bash run-mac.sh`. The script selects `mac-arm64`
(Apple Silicon, Metal) or `mac-x64` (Intel, CPU) and opens the web interface once
the server is ready.

Equivalent invocation on Apple Silicon:

```bash
./mac-arm64/llama-server -m ./model/Ling-3.0-tiny-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --reasoning-preserve -ngl 999 --port 8002
```

### Windows

Double-click `run-windows.bat`. The script probes the real GPU devices
(`--list-devices`): if a Vulkan device is available (NVIDIA, AMD, or Intel), it
uses `win-vulkan` with full GPU offload; otherwise it falls back to `win-cpu`.
To force a backend, create an empty file named `USE_VULKAN` or `USE_CPU` in the
folder.

Equivalent invocation with the Vulkan backend:

```bat
win-vulkan\llama-server.exe -m .\model\Ling-3.0-tiny-Q4_K_M.gguf --reasoning-preserve -ngl 999 --port 8002
```

### Verifying that it runs

- Web interface: <http://127.0.0.1:8002>
- Health: <http://127.0.0.1:8002/health> → `{"status":"ok"}`
- OpenAI-compatible API: <http://127.0.0.1:8002/v1>

The default port is 8002; if it is busy, the scripts switch to 8010 and print the
address. Stop the server with Ctrl+C. Prefer `127.0.0.1` over `localhost` in
tools and scripts: `localhost` may resolve to IPv6 `::1`, which llama.cpp does
not listen on by default.

## Tuning the server

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `-m PATH` | Model file to load |
| `--reasoning-preserve` | Keep the model's reasoning trace in `reasoning_content` (required for the Zed setup below) |
| `-ngl N` | Layers offloaded to the GPU; `999` = all |
| `--n-cpu-moe N` (`-ncmoe N`) | MoE expert layers kept in system RAM (VRAM savings) |
| `-c N` | Context length in tokens (default 4096) |
| `--port N` | Server port (scripts use 8002, fallback 8010) |

### GPU offload: `-ngl 999`

`-ngl 999` pushes every layer to the GPU (Vulkan on Windows, Metal on Apple
Silicon). On the demo machine it ran about 2× faster than CPU. With the GPU
backend, always keep `-ngl 999`; on a GPU short on VRAM, reduce the memory of the
*experts* instead, not the number of GPU layers.

### MoE offload for low VRAM: `--n-cpu-moe`

Ling-3.0-tiny is a mixture-of-experts model: it stores 7.9B parameters but only
activates ~1.3B per token. The server keeps all expert weights in memory, and by
default tries to place everything in VRAM. When the 4.5 GB model does not fit on
the card, `--n-cpu-moe N` (short form `-ncmoe N`) keeps the expert weights of the
top N layers in system RAM, while attention, the router, and the shared experts
stay on the GPU.

```bash
llama-server -m ./model/Ling-3.0-tiny-Q4_K_M.gguf --reasoning-preserve -ngl 999 -ncmoe 24 --port 8002
```

Tuning rule: raise N until the model loads without spilling VRAM, then step back
one notch. Each layer moved to the CPU makes token generation slower when a token
picks an expert stored in RAM, so the smallest N that fits gives the best speed.
The exact number depends on your card; watch the VRAM figure printed at startup.

### Context size: `-c`

The server starts with a 4096-token context, which is short for a tutoring
conversation. Extend it at launch, for example `-c 8192`. A larger context uses
more RAM and VRAM. Set the same value in the Zed configuration (next section);
the two must agree.

## Connecting the server to Zed

Start the server first, with `--reasoning-preserve` and the `-c` value you chose.
In Zed, add an *OpenAI-compatible* provider from the Agent settings
(`agent: open settings`, *Add Provider*): API URL
`http://127.0.0.1:8002/v1`, model `Ling-3.0-tiny`. Any API key works (`local`),
since llama.cpp does not validate it.

The same provider in `settings.json`:

```json
{
  "language_models": {
    "openai_compatible": {
      "llamacpp": {
        "api_url": "http://127.0.0.1:8002/v1",
        "available_models": [
          {
            "name": "Ling-3.0-tiny",
            "display_name": "Ling 3.0 Tiny (local)",
            "max_tokens": 8192,
            "max_output_tokens": 2048,
            "capabilities": {
              "tools": true,
              "images": false,
              "parallel_tool_calls": false,
              "prompt_cache_key": false,
              "chat_completions": true,
              "interleaved_reasoning": true,
              "max_tokens_parameter": true
            }
          }
        ]
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Meaningful fields for this endpoint:

- `api_url`: the OpenAI-compatible base URL of the local server.
- `capabilities.chat_completions: true`: use the `/chat/completions` endpoint.
- `capabilities.interleaved_reasoning: true`: send the reasoning trace back to
  the model as a dedicated `reasoning_content` field on the next turn. This flag
  is required here. The server stores the thinking trace in `reasoning_content`
  (enabled by `--reasoning-preserve`); dropping the trace between turns degrades
  the tutor's thread noticeably. Zed re-injects it, the same mechanism as a
  scripted multi-turn exchange.
- `capabilities.max_tokens_parameter: true`: send the output-token limit as
  `max_tokens`, which llama.cpp expects, instead of `max_completion_tokens`.
- `max_tokens`: the model's context window. Set it to the `-c` value you pass at
  launch; the two must match.

Select **Ling-3.0-tiny** in the Agent panel. The model reasons by default, and
Zed shows the trace (thinking) as it does for other reasoning models.
